<meta>continues from previous page: ...And for the sake of self-protection. May that <term>camasa</term> <gloss>sacrificial vessel</gloss> of yours, the instrument of consumption, not leak; may it not pass away. The mantra-seeing seer says, "Lead that."</meta>

I offer the eye, the mouth, and the beginning of the sacrifice, along with speech, hearing, and the mind.
May the gods, acting with goodwill, come to this sacrifice stretched out by <term>Viśvakarman</term> <gloss>the all-creating deity</gloss>. 5

The eye, the beginning, the mouth, along with speech, with hearing, with the mind, I offer.
To this sacrifice, stretched out by <term>Viśvakarman</term>, may the gods come, acting with goodwill. 5

This stanza has been explained previously (Atharva Veda 2.35.5). I offer the senses, beginning with the eye, as well as the mind, as they pertain to the sacrifice, and I make them inclined toward it. The meaning of this is that the gods, who are the world-creators, should come—that is, arrive—at this mental sacrifice that has been stretched out, meaning extended, by the deity <term>Viśvakarman</term>, and they should act with goodwill, as if they were of pure mind.

Those who are the officiating priests of the gods, and those who are worthy of the sacrifice, and those to whom the share of the offering is made.
May all the gods come to this sacrifice with their wives, and let them rejoice with brilliance. 6

Those who are the officiating priests of the gods, those who are worthy of the sacrifice, and those to whom the share of the oblation is offered.
May all the gods—however many there are—come to this sacrifice with their wives, such as <term>Indrāṇī</term> <gloss>the wife of Indra</gloss>, and let them rejoice, being satisfied by the reception of the oblation, through their own brilliance. 6

Thus ends the fourth hymn in the seventh section.

The hymn beginning with "You, O Agni, are the guardian of vows" is prescribed for use when there is an error in the new-moon or full-moon sacrifice, for the offering of clarified butter, or for the pacifying installation of fuel. It is indeed codified by <term>Kauśika</term> <gloss>the author of the Kausika-sutra</gloss> in the <term>Samhitāvidhi</term> <gloss>ritual manual for the collection of mantras</gloss>.

<note>1. <term>Kriyate</term> (is made) in versions A, Bb, C, R, and Sm; <term>kriyate</term> in version Cs; <term>kṛṇute</term> (performs for himself) in version D. 2. <term>patnībhiḥ</term> (with wives) in A, K, Km, V, Dc; <term>patnībhiḥ</term> in Bb, Sm; <term>patnībhir-aitya</term> (having come with wives) in R; <term>patnībhiḥ</term> to <term>patnībhiḥ</term> in C; <term>patnībhire</term> in D; <term>patnībhir-aitya</term> in Cs. 3. <term>tviṣā mād-</term> (rejoice with brilliance) in A, R, Cs; <term>tviṣā mād-</term> in Bb, C, D, Sm; <term>tviṣā mādayantām</term> (let them rejoice) in V, K, Km; <term>tviṣā mādayatām</term> to <term>tviṣā mādayantām</term> in Dc; <term>devāḥ samiṣāḥ</term> (gods with food) in RW; <term>devā haviṣā</term> (gods with oblation) in W; see also Kausika 1.148.3c.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the invocation of gods to the sacrificial ritual and details the roles of officiating priests and the significance of offerings, concluding with a reference to the ritual rules set by Kausika.</summary>
<keywords>Vedic sacrifice, Viśvakarman, priests, oblation, ritual correction, Kausika-sutra, gods</keywords>
